title: What “Form” of Uncertainty Does Conformal Prediction Quantify?

paper.title: What “Form” of Uncertainty Does Conformal Prediction Quantify?
paper.abstract: Abstract Conformal prediction (CP) is a post-hoc calibration method that returns prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and the size of the output set is often interpreted as a notion of uncertainty. We show that the difference in set size between full and split CP is directly connected to Bayesian posterior variance, which is the epistemic uncertainty of the model. Essentially, this difference in set size is an aggregation of two opposite effects: (1) better model accuracy and therefore smaller set size achieved by training over extra calibration points, and (2) the “formability” of the model at test point towards every possible label. The latter effect vanishes with stronger models or more calibration data (as epistemic uncertainty is known for that behavior). It turns out that the model’s formability itself (without the quantization effect of prediction sets, and through estimating the posterior variance) is a useful tool to quantify the epistemic uncertainty. In our empirical evaluation it performs on par with the state of the art in many setups.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A model’s prediction can be uncertain, either since the data is hard to predict (aleatoric), or because the model is not confident in its prediction due to lack of information (epistemic). Conformal prediction (CP) is a widely used approach in risk-critical applications where quantifying total predictive uncertainty is crucial. Given any model f ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝜽 ) f(\cdot;{\bm{\theta}}) , CP returns a prediction set 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝒙 n + 1 ) {\mathcal{C}}({\bm{x}}_{n+1}) for a test point 𝒙 n + 1 {\bm{x}}_{n+1} that is guaranteed to include the true label with user-specified probability 1 − α 1-\alpha . This guarantee is distribution-free; namely, it holds regardless of the underlying data distribution, or the model family ( Angelopoulos et al., 2024 ) . CP requires an exchangeable set of calibration points, and can be applied in two ways: (i) fine-tuning the model jointly on the calibration set and the test point for every possible pseudo-label (full CP), or (ii) only evaluating the model on the calibration points (split CP). Full CP is known to be more data-efficient, which is particularly appealing in cases with label scarcity ( Lei et al., 2018 ) (e.g. semi-supervised graph node classification). The argument is that in these settings the data is not divided into separate training and calibration sets, which potentially results in better model performance, and smaller sets. In contrast, Zong and Xu (2025) show that full CP doesn’t always outperform split CP without specifying a definitive reason, leaving this question open: when and by how much full CP can be more efficient, and what can be concluded from their performance gap? It turns out (as shown in Fig. 1 , and Fig. 2 ), the performance gap (set size difference) reduces with a larger dataset (calibration, or training), and a lower feature dimension. Intuitively, while in most cases a larger dataset (combination of training and calibration) improves the model’s performance, fine-tuning on the test point with a pseudo-label deforms the model towards that label. The strength of this deformation is governed by the calibration density, and the confidence from pretraining both as resisting factors. Strong deformation includes wrong pseudo-labels in the set, resulting in worse overall performance. In particular, we define formability at a test point, as the difference between the predictive probability of any label between two models: one fine-tuned on a calibration set, and the other on the union of the calibration set and the pseudo-labeled test point (on that label). Under Bayesian training, where the epistemic uncertainty is quantified as the disagreement among the plausible (under the posterior) parameters, we show that formability is directly related to the epistemic uncertainty of the predictive distribution at the test point; namely we bound the posterior variance, by a function of formability. This also shows the reason why by increasing calibration set size the difference between full and split CP disappears: the formability (epistemic uncertainty) is known to reduce with more data.

sections.heading: 3.1 Motivating Experiment
sections.text: First we evaluate the claim that “in label scarcity, full CP outperforms split CP” by comparing full and split conformal prediction on two simple setups with images ( CIFAR-10 ; Krizhevsky, 2009 ), and graphs ( CoraML ; Bojchevski and Günnemann, 2018 ). It is already mentioned in a couple of works that in some cases full CP is not better than split CP in set size ( Barber et al., 2023 ; Zong and Xu, 2025 , e.g.,) . As shown in Fig. 1 , however, by increasing the calibration set size, or reducing the feature dimension (using PCA), the performance gap is reduced, until the two methods cross over. These two observations suggest that the performance gap is not governed by the amount of data alone, but by how strongly the model is already determined around the test point. Notably, the argument of “full CP leverages a better model” still serves as a lower bound on the set size, which full CP converges to, by increasing the size of the calibration set. Figure 3: The formability p n , c ​ ( c ∣ 𝒙 ) − p n ​ ( c ∣ 𝒙 ) p_{n,c}(c\mid{\bm{x}})-p_{n}(c\mid{\bm{x}}) by fine-tuning on the pseudo-label c c at the test point (star), in a dense [left pair], and a sparse [right pair] (calibration) neighborhood. Pairs are a correct, and a wrong label c c . Calibration points are colored by the shift of their true score (negligible at many points), and the bars report A n , c A_{n,c} , Φ n , c \Phi_{n,c} , and T n , c T_{n,c} from Eq. 2 . An intuitive explanation for such behaviour is that when the training and calibration data is scarce, the model can still be deformed towards any label at the test point. Therefore, it is very easy for every (true or false) label of 𝒙 n + 1 {\bm{x}}_{n+1} to pull its own score above the threshold. To observe this mechanism in isolation, we show a synthesized setup where every score is visible on a 2-dim landscape ( Fig. 3 , details are in § C.1.1 ). We compare a test point inside a dense calibration neighborhood to one in a sparse support. In all cases, fine-tuning on the pseudo-label deforms the predictive distribution towards the pseudo-label. However, for the one in the dense region, the calibration density resists this deformation, and the self-pull remains small. In the sparse region there are no proximate data to resist. Hence, every pseudo-label pulls its own score above the threshold easily. As a result, the wrong label enters the full set exactly where the model was free to deform. Therefore the performance gap in CPs is governed by the significance of the new test data point w.r.t. the model: how much the model can deform at that point (which is inversely related to the size of 𝒟 n {\mathcal{D}}_{n} , and the strength of the pretrained model as a resisting factor). Namely, this deformation is connected to the epistemic uncertainty – a model with more knowledge (training, and calibration data) is harder to form towards wrong labels. This direct connection between formability and epistemic uncertainty is particularly important when it compares with methods like softmax entropy. Naturally, the softmax entropy, when evaluated on a single predictor can not distinguish between the two types of uncertainty. Fig. 4 shows that by replicating the setup from Fig. 3 while moving the generative Gaussians close to each other. At the center, the epistemic uncertainty decrease, while aleatoric uncertainty increase. On a single label distribution however, it is presented as [ 1 / k ] k [1/k]_{k} the entire time. Therefore the softmax entropy does not react to this change, while the formability variance does.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We investigated the performance gap between full, and split conformal prediction. We showed that the gap is the resultant of two opposite effects: adapting the model on the calibration set (more data resulting in better model, and hence smaller sets), and forming it towards each pseudo-label at the test point. Under Bayesian learning, the second effect (formability) is directly tied to posterior predictive variance, and fades as the calibration posterior concentrates. This explains why full CP can become more efficient when the model is already well determined around the test point, and in sparse regions it performs poorly. However, this gap suggest to use formability as a measure of epistemic uncertainty that carries much more information compared to set size (due to the 0/1 binarization). Our experiments on images and graphs show its value for detecting prediction errors; and to some degree, ood detection. In many benchmarks, formability is on par with the best of the existing uncertainty quantification methods, and in some cases it outperforms them. Limitations. The most important limitation is the computational cost of refitting the model on every candidate label. Additionally our analysis, and definition of formability is based on the softmax score function. CP itself is agnostic to the choice of score function, and scores like APS also can lead to meaningful interpretations of the full-vs-split gap. We leave this for future work. Additionally, conformal prediction assumes exchangeability of the data, which is not always satisfied in practice, specifically for uncertainty quantification use cases. Formability implicitly assume that refits are able to reach the MAP estimate. This could challenge the quality in overparameterized models, or in wrong early stopping scenarios. Potentially our language model experiments are affected by this.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Works
sections.text: Conformal prediction. CP ( Vovk et al., 2005 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2024 ) is considered a distribution-free uncertainty quantification technique, where the prediction sets are guaranteed to cover the true label with high probability. With that, many consider the size of the prediction set to represent how uncertain the model is on a specific input. While the method works with any model, and any score function, there are many works designing various scores to improve the set size efficiency, adaptivity, and approximation of conditional coverage ( Romano et al., 2020 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2021 ; Zargarbashi et al., 2023 ) . We use the basic threshold prediction sets ( Sadinle et al., 2019 ) since it directly connects to the predictive distribution of the model which can connect perfectly with our decomposition in § 3 , and through which we bound the epistemic uncertainty. In § C.1.6 we repeat our experiments under an adaptive (rank-based) score, where the full–split gap is wider, and never closes. While full and split conformal prediction are two endpoints of a computational cost spectrum, there are other variants such as Jackknife+ ( Barber et al., 2021 ) in between. There are techniques that approximate full CP with lower computational cost ( Bhatt et al., 2021 ; Abad Martinez et al., 2023 ) , through influence functions ( Koh and Liang, 2017 ) . Both directions are outside of our focus, as we address the fundamental difference between full and split CP. CP and epistemic uncertainty. Javanmardi et al. (2026) ; Cruz Cabezas et al. (2025) incorporate a second-order distribution (which contains explicit epistemic uncertainty) into conformal prediction. In the reverse direction, Chau et al. (2026) ; Correia et al. (2024) provide interpretations of split conformal prediction in uncertainty quantification; one through connecting split CP to imprecise integral probability metrics, and the other through information theory. In contrast, we provide a direct connection between the difference of full and split CP set size and the epistemic uncertainty, by bounding the posterior variance of the predictive distribution. Our work connects three arguments: (i) When does full CP outperform split CP? Inconsistencies in comparison are mentioned by Barber et al. (2023) and extensively studied by Zong and Xu (2025) . However, neither work discusses what the underlying factor is that governs this difference. We show that the unexpected inefficiency in full CP set size stems from the formability of the model at the test point. (ii) We show that, in a Bayesian framework, the formability is directly related to the posterior variance (epistemic uncertainty). The concept of deterministic formability itself is not entirely new. Bibas et al. (2019) define a learnability measure (regret) as the log sum of the predictive probabilities θ ^ n , c \hat{\theta}_{n,c} normalized by the probabilities from θ ^ n \hat{\theta}_{n} . However, its connection with Bayesian posterior variance, comparison with deterministic Laplace approximation through basin decomposition ( Daxberger et al., 2021 ) , or its influence on full conformal prediction do not follow automatically. (iii) We show that on larger models and various tasks this notion of formability still can be used as a practical tool to quantify epistemic uncertainty. Our work also connects with many other uncertainty quantification approaches. While the posterior distribution of parameters is a canonical way to quantify epistemic uncertainty, on larger models it is computationally near-impossible to compute. Laplace Redux ( Daxberger et al., 2021 ) approximates this distribution as a Gaussian around the MAP estimate. However, as we show in Prop. 3.3 it is agnostic to other basins of attraction, and therefore miscalculates the epistemic uncertainty where other highly plausible basins disagree with the current predictive distribution. A remedy to that is MC-dropout ( Gal and Ghahramani, 2016 ) , and ensemble training ( Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017 ) , which are parameter centric approximations. Formability however is a data-centric approximation. On computation, the comparison depends on whether multiple model inference or test-time training is more favorable. Schweighofer et al. (2023) instead searches for adversarial models with high disagreement to the baseline, while attaining high posterior plausibility. In comparison, formability is a local measure, searching for such models through retraining. The comparison results as shown in Fig. 17 are very close. Our ultimate goal is also not to come up with a new notion of uncertainty, but to showcase what is the underlying uncertainty quantification in conformal prediction.

sections.heading: C.1.4 The Frozen Image Backbones
sections.text: Every image experiment in this paper trains a small head on top of a frozen ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) -pretrained backbone, and the feature space from which the formability is defined is the output of this backbone (this especially matters for CIFAR-10 experiments with feature reduction). The ImageNet output layer is removed, the remaining network embeds each image once, and only the head is trained, or refitted. The backbone itself is never updated, which helps us to reduce the cost of per-candidate refit from the entire model to only the head. sections.heading: C.1.5 Full vs. Split CP over the Feature Dimension
sections.text: Setup. We use a two-layer GCN ( Kipf and Welling, 2017 ) over the 2879 2879 -dimensional bag-of-words node features of CoraML , and a two-layer MLP over the 512 512 -dimensional embedding of a frozen ImageNet -pretrained ResNet-18 for CIFAR-10 . Full CP trains the model from initialization on the training set, the calibration set, and the pseudo-labeled test point. We reduce the features by PCA to K ∈ { 32 , 16 , 8 } K\in\{32,16,8\} for CoraML , and K ∈ { 64 , 32 , 16 } K\in\{64,32,16\} for CIFAR-10 , and sweep n cal n_{\mathrm{cal}} , and n tr n_{\mathrm{tr}} . The score is the predictive probability of § 2 , and 1 − α = 0.9 1-\alpha=0.9 . The adaptation floor | 𝒞 B | |{\mathcal{C}}_{B}| is the size of the posterior conformal set 𝒞 𝜽 n ​ ( 𝒙 n + 1 ) {\mathcal{C}}_{{\bm{\theta}}_{n}}({\bm{x}}_{n+1}) i.e. split CP on the model trained on the training, and the calibration set together, which needs a single fit per calibration set, and no per-candidate refit. Results. In Fig. 9 , and Fig. 10 the plots go from the full feature space to the smallest K K . The top row reports the average set size against n cal n_{\mathrm{cal}} , where the hollow markers are the approximate full CP with m = 50 m=50 , and the bottom row reports the empirical coverage of the same sets against the nominal 1 − α 1-\alpha . Full, and split CP are at the nominal level in every panel which shows the sanity of the result. The adaptation floor is not (as expected): it under-covers by a wide margin in the full feature space ( ≈ 0.57 \approx 0.57 on CoraML at n cal = 50 n_{\mathrm{cal}}=50 , and ≈ 0.49 \approx 0.49 on CIFAR-10 at n cal = 100 n_{\mathrm{cal}}=100 ), and it approaches 1 − α 1-\alpha as n cal n_{\mathrm{cal}} grows, or K K shrinks. This is expected, since 𝒞 B {\mathcal{C}}_{B} scores the calibration points it was trained on, and the amount of this optimism is again a formability – now read at the calibration points. Similarly in set size, we observe that by increasing the calibration points, the difference between the two approaches decreases, until full CP crosses the split CP. Notably this effect is more visible in CIFAR-10 than in CoraML . Mainly this is since the training size of the CIFAR-10 is larger than that of CoraML . We also observe that reducing the feature dimension closes the performance gap. An interesting side observation is that the question of whether the full CP is more efficient than the split CP can be answered without the need to compute the full CP. One can simply estimate it with a small sample rate ( m = 50 m=50 ) by computing a leave-one-out refit on the calibration set, and that point alone. This is a relatively cheap operation to check the performance gap, without the need for expensive computation. The method turns out to be a good approximation as shown in both figures (the hollow markers are the approximate full CP with m = 50 m=50 ). We report the extended experiment on the gap | 𝒞 F ​ ( 𝒙 n + 1 ) | − | 𝒞 S ​ ( 𝒙 n + 1 ) | |{\mathcal{C}}^{F}({\bm{x}}_{n+1})|-|{\mathcal{C}}^{S}({\bm{x}}_{n+1})| over a grid of n train n_{\mathrm{train}} , and n cal n_{\mathrm{cal}} , on CoraML ( 2879 2879 -d), and on CIFAR-10 (the 512 512 -d embedding). The results are shown in Fig. 11 . This is also same as our expectation. Another takeaway from this result is that the training set size also decreases the performance, and as the training size increases, the effect of the calibration set size becomes less significant.

sections.text: In this work we focus on threshold prediction sets as the score function ( Sadinle et al., 2019 ) : it directly sets the conformity score to the predictive probability of the candidate label; i.e. s ⁡ ( 𝒙 , y ) = p 𝜽 ​ ( y ∣ 𝒙 ) s({\bm{x}},y)=p_{\bm{\theta}}(y\mid{\bm{x}}) . That object is very easy to work with and it directly connects to the decomposition of Eq. 2 to the updates of the predictive distribution after refits. However, conformal prediction is agnostic to the choice of score, and the same margin-decomposition can apply on other score functions as well. It is an important question to ask what interpretation does the full-split gap (and in particular the margin gap) has under that different score. We repeat the experiment shown in Fig. 10 , this time under the adaptive prediction sets (APS) score ( Romano et al., 2020 ) . Result is shown in Fig. 12 . The score therefore remains a deterministic function of the predictive distribution, and the exchangeability argument is untouched. Everything else – the grid, the test points, the models, and 1 − α = 0.9 1-\alpha=0.9 – is as in Fig. 11 . Result. Split CP is smaller in every cell of both grids, and by a wide margin, and by increasing the training points or calibration points the gap converges to zero. APS can be read as a fractional knapsack problem over the probabilty distribution: take the smallest number of labels (all with equal weight), until 1 − β 1-\beta cumulative probability is captured. Then conformalization (computing the quantile) is an answer to: what cumulative 1 − β 1-\beta in model’s predictive probability can capture the 1 − α 1-\alpha probability in the true distribution. The gap is therefore a measure of how much the model’s predictive distribution is misaligned with the true distribution, and the gap converges to zero as the model sees more labels and becomes better aligned with the true distribution. However deriving the same formability decomposition as in § 3.2 is not straightforward, specially since the score involves the ranking of the labels, and the refit can change this ranking. We leave this as an open question for future work.

sections.heading: C.2 Formability on Language Models
sections.text: For language model tasks, we use four-option question answering: each model assigns probabilities to the answer letters A–D, and the conformal set contains a subset of these letters. We do not evaluate free-form generations. Even keeping most of the parameters frozen, running the same pipeline as the images, and graphs can be significantly more expensive. Therefore we approximate formability by a local update of a LoRA adapter. In general we follow the full conformal approximation from Abad Martinez et al. (2023) , but this time over the LoRA adapter parameters, for the classification task. Setup. We use six model–dataset combinations: Llama-1B, Llama-3B ( Grattafiori and others, 2024 ) , Qwen-1.5B, and Qwen-3B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) on MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) humanities and business, and Llama-1B on MedQA ( Jin et al., 2021 ) and MedMCQA ( Pal et al., 2022 ) . The pretrained language model is frozen, and a LoRA adapter is fitted on 2000 2000 labeled training questions. The LoRA adapter is applied with rank r = 8 r=8 , and scaling α = 16 \alpha=16 , dropout 0, on query and value matrices of the attention layers. The same setup is also used for the ensemble model. From separate pools of 6000 6000 calibration questions, and 800 800 evaluation questions, we vary the calibration set size from 50 50 to 2000 2000 , with 20 20 calibration draws. The score is the probability assigned to an answer letter. Every uncertainty measure ranks the same evaluation questions, using the misclassification AUROC, and selective E-AURC as mentioned in § 4 . Softmax entropy, kNN, Mahalanobis and the ensemble are not computed from p 𝜽 p_{\bm{\theta}} . They come from a separate cached model fitted on the training questions plus one fixed set of calibration questions. Formability is however computed from damped influence steps that start at that same anchor adapter. The comparison is not entirely fair, but it is the best we can do given the expensive computational cost of the refits on LLMs. Approximate refits. Let 𝜽 ~ n \tilde{\bm{\theta}}_{n} denote the adapter fitted on the training questions, and updated by a single damped influence step over calibration points, and let 𝜽 ~ n , c \tilde{\bm{\theta}}_{n,c} denote the adapter fitted on those same questions plus ( 𝒙 n + 1 , c ) ({\bm{x}}_{n+1},c) . These are the base, and refit whose difference defines formability. The pseudo-labeled test question is the only additional observation. We approximate the two fits by damped influence steps in the adapter parameters ( Koh and Liang, 2017 ; Abad Martinez et al., 2023 ) , rather than optimizing a new adapter for every candidate. In particular, the additional step from the base has the form 𝜽 ~ n , c − 𝜽 ~ n ≈ − 1 N + 1 ​ ( H + λ ​ 𝑰 ) − 1 ​ g c , \tilde{\bm{\theta}}_{n,c}-\tilde{\bm{\theta}}_{n}\ \approx\ -\tfrac{1}{N+1}(H+\lambda{\bm{I}})^{-1}g_{c}, (16) where g c = ∇ 𝜽 ℓ ​ ( 𝒙 n + 1 , c , 𝜽 ref ) g_{c}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell({\bm{x}}_{n+1},c;{\bm{\theta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}) , and 𝜽 ref {\bm{\theta}}_{\mathrm{ref}} is the adapter at which the gradients are cached. Similar to the image and graph experiments, the approximate formability shows a performance that is competitive with the best method and performs better than many other approaches. Soroush H. Zargarbashi Mohammad Sadegh Akhondzadeh Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security University of Cologne Rebekka Burkholz Aleksandar Bojchevski Affiliation: CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security University of Cologne Abstract Conformal prediction (CP) is a post-hoc calibration method that returns prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and the size of the output set is often interpreted as a notion of uncertainty. We show that the difference in set size between full and split CP is directly connected to Bayesian posterior variance, which is the epistemic uncertainty of the model. Essentially, this difference in set size is an aggregation of two opposite effects: (1) better model accuracy and therefore smaller set size achieved by training over extra calibration points, and (2) the “formability” of the model at test point towards every possible label. The latter effect vanishes with stronger models or more calibration data (as epistemic uncertainty is known for that behavior). It turns out that the model’s formability itself (without the quantization effect of prediction sets, and through estimating the posterior variance) is a useful tool to quantify the epistemic uncertainty. In our empirical evaluation it performs on par with the state of the art in many setups. Figure 1: Comparison of full (blue, solid) vs. split (orange, dashed) CP, against the adaptation floor | 𝒞 B | |{\mathcal{C}}_{B}| (see § 3 ), over n cal n_{\mathrm{cal}} and feature dimension K K , and for [Left] CoraML (transductive node-classification, GCN), and [Right] CIFAR-10. The approximation is with m = 50 m=50 samples (see § 4 ). 1 Introduction A model’s prediction can be uncertain, either since the data is hard to predict (aleatoric), or because the model is not confident in its prediction due to lack of information (epistemic). Conformal prediction (CP) is a widely used approach in risk-critical applications where quantifying total predictive uncertainty is crucial. Given any model f ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝜽 ) f(\cdot;{\bm{\theta}}) , CP returns a prediction set 𝒞 ⁡ ( 𝒙 n + 1 ) {\mathcal{C}}({\bm{x}}_{n+1}) for a test point 𝒙 n + 1 {\bm{x}}_{n+1} that is guaranteed to include the true label with user-specified probability 1 − α 1-\alpha . This guarantee is distribution-free; namely, it holds regardless of the underlying data distribution, or the model family ( Angelopoulos et al., 2024 ) . CP requires an exchangeable set of calibration points, and can be applied in two ways: (i) fine-tuning the model jointly on the calibration set and the test point for every possible pseudo-label (full CP), or (ii) only evaluating the model on the calibration points (split CP). Full CP is known to be more data-efficient, which is particularly appealing in cases with label scarcity ( Lei et al., 2018 ) (e.g. semi-supervised graph node classification). The argument is that in these settings the data is not divided into separate training and calibration sets, which potentially results in better model performance, and smaller sets. In contrast, Zong and Xu (2025) show that full CP doesn’t always outperform split CP without specifying a definitive reason, leaving this question open: when and by how much full CP can be more efficient, and what can be concluded from their performance gap? It turns out (as shown in Fig. 1 , and Fig. 2 ), the performance gap (set size difference) reduces with a larger dataset (calibration, or training), and a lower feature dimension. Intuitively, while in most cases a larger dataset (combination of training and calibration) improves the model’s performance, fine-tuning on the test point with a pseudo-label deforms the model towards that label. The strength of this deformation is governed by the calibration density, and the confidence from pretraining both as resisting factors. Strong deformation includes wrong pseudo-labels in the set, resulting in worse overall performance. In particular, we define formability at a test point, as the difference between the predictive probability of any label between two models: one fine-tuned on a calibration set, and the other on the union of the calibration set and the pseudo-labeled test point (on that label). Under Bayesian training, where the epistemic uncertainty is quantified as the disagreement among the plausible (under the posterior) parameters, we show that formability is directly related to the epistemic uncertainty of the predictive distribution at the test point; namely we bound the posterior variance, by a function of formability. This also shows the reason why by increasing calibration set size the difference between full and split CP disappears: the formability (epistemic uncertainty) is known to reduce with more data. 2 Background Let f ⁡ ( ⋅ , 𝜽 ) f(\cdot;{\bm{\theta}}) be a pretrained model from the family ℱ {\mathcal{F}} specified by the parameters 𝜽 {\bm{\theta}} . We use p 𝜽 ​ ( y ∣ 𝒙 ) p_{\bm{\theta}}(y\mid{\bm{x}}) for the predictive label distribution of f f at the input 𝒙 {\bm{x}} . Let 𝒟 n = { ( 𝒙 i , y i ) } i = 1 n {\mathcal{D}}_{n}=\{({\bm{x}}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be a holdout calibration set jointly exchangeable with the test point ( 𝒙 n + 1 , y n + 1 ) ({\bm{x}}_{n+1},y_{n+1}) . We showed that the gap is the resultant of two opposite effects: adapting the model on the calibration set (more data resulting in better model, and hence smaller sets), and forming it towards each pseudo-label at the test point.
